name: Arkippus
title: Fellow Worker and Church Servant in Colosse
summary: Archippus was a Christian coworker who held an important service role in the church at Colossae. Paul refers to him as "our fellow soldier" (Greek: systratiōtēs, literally "fellow soldier") in the greeting of the letter to Philemon, where he is mentioned together with Philemon and Apphia. Tradition has assumed that the three belonged to the same household, but this is not directly confirmed by the biblical text. In Colossians, Paul gives a reminder through the church to Archippus to see that he completes the service (diakonia) he has received in the Lord – an exhortation that testifies to his bearing significant responsibility in the local Christian community, possibly in connection with Epaphras' absence.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as a Fellow Worker
keyEvents.description: Paul greets Arkippus in the letter to Philemon and calls him 'our fellow worker,' indicating his active role in advancing the gospel and fighting for the faith alongside Paul.

keyEvents.title: Exhortation to Complete the Service
keyEvents.description: In Colossians, Paul urges the church to tell Arkippus to make sure he completes the service (diakonia) he has received in the Lord. This suggests that Arkippus had been given a specific assignment or calling that required faithful perseverance.

keyEvents.title: Part of the House Church in Colosse
keyEvents.description: Arkippus is mentioned together with Philemon and Apphia in connection with the house church that gathered in Philemon's home in Colossae, which suggests that he held a central place in this fellowship.

versions.summary: Arkippus was a Christian leader in the church at Colossae, possibly the son of Philemon and Apphia. Paul called him a 'fellow soldier' and urged him to complete the ministry he had received in the Lord.
versions.title: Fellow Soldier in the Faith
versions.reason: [minor] The Bible does not explicitly state that Philemon was Archippus's father. Philemon 1:2 mentions Philemon, Appia, and Archippus together, but the relationship is uncertain. Many scholars assume this, but it should be reflected as a possibility, not as an established fact. It is better to set father to null and mention the possibility in the summary.; [minor] Similarly, it is not explicitly confirmed in the Bible that Appia was Archippus's mother. This is a common assumption based on the three being mentioned together in Philemon 1:2, but it remains speculation. It is better to set mother to null.; [minor] The role 'fellow soldier' (gr. systratiōtēs) is the most explicit designation Paul uses for Archippus and should be included as a role. 'Servant' is somewhat vague – 'preacher' or 'church servant' may be more precise given the context in Col 4:17 where Paul refers to a diakonia (service).; [minor] The summary is well written but could be improved by clarifying that the family relationship with Philemon and Appia is a traditional assumption, not biblically confirmed.; [major] Footnotes covering interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details about Archippus are missing. The Greek word 'systratiōtēs' (fellow soldier) should be explained, and the traditional assumption of family relationship should be illuminated.

versions.summary: Arkippus was a Christian leader in the church at Colossae whom Paul called a 'fellow soldier' (Greek: systratiōtēs). He is mentioned in the greeting of the letter to Philemon alongside Philemon and Apphia, and tradition has assumed that the three were a family, although the Bible does not explicitly confirm this. In Colossians, Paul urges the church to tell Arkippus to see to it that he completes the ministry (diakonia) he has received in the Lord, suggesting that he had an important mission in the local church.
versions.title: Fellow Soldier in the Faith
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Fellow Soldier in the Faith' is good, but could be refined slightly to reflect that he also had a service role in the church. A more comprehensive title might be 'Fellow Soldier and Church Servant in Colossae'.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat unspecified. The biblical text does not provide explicit grounds for calling Archippus a 'leader', although the exhortation in Col 4:17 suggests an important service role. It may be more precise to replace 'leader' with 'church servant' or retain 'church servant', which already covers this.

footnotes.text: The Greek word 'systratiōtēs' (συστρατιώτης), used of Arkippus in Philemon 1:2, literally means 'fellow soldier' and is used by Paul as a metaphor for someone who fights alongside him in the service of the faith. Paul uses the same word about Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:25.

The tradition that Arkippus was the son of Philemon and Apphia stems from the fact that all three are mentioned together in the greeting of Philemon 1:1–2, where Apphia is referred to as 'our sister'. Some early church fathers, including Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458), assumed a family bond, but the biblical text does not explicitly confirm this.

The exhortation in Colossians 4:17 that Arkippus should 'see to it that he completes the ministry (diakonia) he has received in the Lord' has been the subject of much discussion. Some scholars believe it may refer to a specific task related to the church at Colossae, possibly following Epaphras's absence. Others have suggested that the ministry was connected to the church at Laodicea, mentioned in Col 4:15–16.

Colossae was a city in Phrygia in western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). The city lay by the Lycus River, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. In Paul's time, Colossae was already in decline compared to neighboring cities, yet it still had an active Christian church.

The name Arkippus (Ἄρχιππος) is composed of the Greek words 'archē' (beginning, rule, leadership) and 'hippos' (horse), and means approximately 'lord of horses' or 'one who rules over horses'. It was a common Greek name, suggesting that Arkippus had a Hellenistic background.
